summary: The BGP Monitoring Protocol is used to monitor BGP sessions and provide a convenient interface for obtaining route views, replacing earlier screen scraping. This standards-track RFC aims to keep BMP simple, useful and easy to implement. It is not a routing protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) lets a router send a monitoring station information about its BGP peers and routes. The station receives a starting snapshot and then updates, but it does not send BMP messages back to the router.

subtitle: A one-way stream from a router that gives a monitoring station BGP route and session information.

tldr.problem: Operators and researchers want to inspect BGP routing information and updates received by a router. Before BMP, the RFC says screen scraping was the most common way to get these views.
tldr.mechanism: A router sends BMP messages over TCP to a monitoring station. The stream includes peer events, an initial route dump, ongoing route changes, and optional statistics or message copies.
tldr.outcome: BMP provides a monitoring interface and is explicitly not a routing protocol. RFC 7854 is updated by RFC 8671, RFC 9069, RFC 9515, and RFC 9736.

today: RFC 7854 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8671, RFC 9069, RFC 9515, and RFC 9736. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What BMP Lets a Station Observe
sections.content:
The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) gives ongoing access to a router's Adj-RIB-In and a periodic dump of selected statistics. Adj-RIB-In is the routing information advertised by peers before the router applies inbound policy. The RFC also defines a post-policy view, after inbound policy but before route selection forms the Loc-RIB.

BMP was designed as a simple monitoring interface and is not suitable for routing. Its goal is to let a monitoring station obtain route views without extracting them from a router's screen.
sections.plainLanguage: BMP lets a router report routes it receives from its BGP peers and, if configured, routes after inbound policy. It is for monitoring those routes, not for making routing decisions between routers.

sections.title: The Router-to-Station Session
sections.content:
BMP runs over TCP. The RFC specifies that no BMP message is sent from the monitoring station to the router; the router sends the monitoring stream. Configuration determines which party opens the TCP connection and which party listens.

Once connected, the router begins with an Initiation message. It then reports each monitored BGP peer in the Established state, sends that peer's initial routes, and marks the end of each peer's initial dump with End-of-RIB. Incremental route changes follow. A session ends when TCP closes; the router may send a Termination message first.

The RFC suggests exponential connection retry backoff, with an initial 30 seconds and a maximum of 720 seconds. It also recommends limits on simultaneous connections and session establishment rates.
sections.plainLanguage: The router opens or accepts a TCP connection according to configuration, then sends its information in one direction. It introduces itself, reports peers and their routes, and continues with updates.

sections.title: Common and Per-Peer Headers
sections.content:
Every BMP message starts with a common header containing a one-byte Version, a four-byte Message Length, and a one-byte Message Type. This specification uses version 3. A receiver MUST ignore message types it does not recognize.

Most messages also have a per-peer header. It identifies the peer type and address, AS number, BGP identifier, and timestamp, and includes flags. The V flag marks an IPv6 peer address; L distinguishes post-policy information from pre-policy information; A marks the legacy two-byte AS_PATH format.

The 16-byte Peer Address field holds IPv6 addresses directly. For IPv4, the address occupies the last four bytes and the remaining bytes are zero-filled. A peer distinguisher helps distinguish peers in separate address domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The common header tells a station how long a message is and what kind it is. A per-peer header on most messages identifies the BGP peer that supplied the information.

sections.title: Seven BMP Message Types
sections.content:
BMP defines seven message types, numbered from 0 through 6. Route Monitoring carries route information; Statistics Report carries counters and gauges; Peer Down and Peer Up report peer-session changes; Initiation describes the router; Termination gives a reason for closing; and Route Mirroring carries copies of received BGP messages.

A Peer Down notification implicitly withdraws that peer's routes, so an implementation may omit separate withdraw messages. An Initiation message must be first after the TCP session comes up. A Termination message includes a required reason and is followed by closure of the TCP session.
sections.plainLanguage: The message types report routes, statistics, peer changes, router information, and session closure. Route Mirroring is a separate message for copying received BGP messages.

sections.title: Route Snapshots, Updates, and Mirroring
sections.content:
Route Monitoring first sends a snapshot of each monitored peer's Adj-RIB-In, then carries ongoing changes in BGP Update messages. The router may report pre-policy routes, post-policy routes, or both; the L flag identifies the view. The initial dump and updates can overlap, so a station must reconcile them.

Route Monitoring is state-compressed: the router may report only the final state when a route changes more than once before reporting. The message may also differ from the original BGP message. Route Mirroring provides verbatim copies, but the RFC warns that buffering them may require unbounded storage and does not recommend this mode unless implementers have weighed its effects.
sections.plainLanguage: Route Monitoring reports the current route state and later changes, but it may combine changes instead of copying every received message. Route Mirroring can copy messages exactly, with resource costs that the RFC warns about.

sections.title: Statistics and Multiple BGP Instances
sections.content:
Statistics Reports are optional. If sent, each report MUST contain at least one statistic. The RFC defines counters and gauges for items such as rejected prefixes, duplicate updates, route counts, and updates treated as withdrawals; unknown statistic types are ignored.

BMP describes one BGP instance. A router with multiple BGP instances should use multiple BMP instances and make their Initiation messages distinguishable. Locally originated routes can be represented as sent by the router to itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can report counts and route totals as well as route updates. Each BGP instance has its own BMP stream so the station can tell them apart.

sections.title: Protecting the Monitoring Session
sections.content:
BMP exposes a full or continuous view of a BGP speaker's routes, which may reveal information that is not otherwise available. The RFC recommends manual configuration of the monitored and monitoring devices.

BMP itself provides neither authentication nor confidentiality. Without mutual authentication, an attacker could impersonate a router or monitoring station. Without confidentiality, an attacker could read or tamper with information in transit. The RFC identifies IPsec in tunnel mode with pre-shared keys as an option when these protections are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: BMP can reveal the routes a router knows, and it does not protect the connection by itself. Use a transport protection method when the information or the identity of either endpoint must be protected.
